section.title: The Council at Jerusalem
section.sectionRationale: The open door to the Gentiles forces the church's deepest question: must a Gentile become a Jew, keeping the law of Moses and circumcision, in order to be saved? The apostles and elders gather in Jerusalem to decide. Peter, Paul, Barnabas, and James testify that God saves Jew and Gentile alike by grace through faith, and the council frees the Gentiles from the yoke of the law while asking them, for the sake of fellowship, to abstain from a few things that would gravely offend Jewish believers. It is the hinge on which the gospel of grace turns.
section.thesis: Salvation is by the grace of the Lord Jesus through faith, not by circumcision or the law of Moses, and so the church, led by the Spirit, refuses to lay the law's yoke on Gentile believers, asking of them only what love and fellowship require.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the dispute over circumcision; the council's testimony from Peter, Barnabas and Paul, and James; the letter to the Gentile believers with its four requests; and the joy at Antioch as the decision is delivered.

units.label: The dispute over circumcision
units.note: must Gentiles keep the law to be saved?

verses.text: Then some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, “Unless you are {{peritemno|circumcised}} according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.”
And after engaging these men in sharp debate, Paul and Barnabas were appointed, along with some other believers, to go up to Jerusalem to see the apostles and elders about this question.
Sent on their way by the church, they passed through Phoenicia and Samaria, recounting the conversion of the Gentiles and bringing great joy to all the brothers.
On their arrival in Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church and apostles and elders, to whom they reported all that God had done through them.
But some believers from the party of the Pharisees stood up and declared, “The Gentiles must be circumcised and required to obey the law of Moses.”

units.label: Peter's testimony: saved by grace
units.note: no distinction; hearts cleansed by faith

verses.text: So the apostles and elders met to look into this matter.

After much discussion, Peter got up and said to them, “Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you that the Gentiles would hear from my lips the message of the gospel and believe.
And God, who knows the heart, showed His approval by giving the Holy Spirit to them, just as He did to us.
He made no distinction between us and them, for He cleansed their hearts by {{pistis|faith}}.
Now then, why do you test God by placing on the necks of the disciples a {{zygos|yoke}} that neither we nor our fathers have been able to bear?
On the contrary, we believe it is through the {{charis|grace}} of the Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are.”

units.label: James and the witness of the prophets
units.note: God rebuilds David's tent to gather the nations

verses.text: The whole assembly fell silent as they listened to Barnabas and Paul describing the signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them.
When they had finished speaking, James declared, “Brothers, listen to me!
Simon has told us how God first visited the Gentiles to take from them a people to be His own.
The words of the prophets agree with this, as it is written:
‘After this I will return and rebuild the fallen tent of David. Its ruins I will rebuild, and I will restore it,
so that the remnant of men may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by My name, says the Lord who does these things
that have been known for ages.’
It is my judgment, therefore, that we should not cause trouble for the Gentiles who are turning to God.
Instead, we should write and tell them to abstain from food polluted by idols, from sexual immorality, from the meat of strangled animals, and from blood.
For Moses has been proclaimed in every city from ancient times and is read in the synagogues on every Sabbath.”

units.label: The letter to the Gentile believers
units.note: it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us

verses.text: Then the apostles and elders, with the whole church, decided to select men from among them to send to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. They chose Judas called Barsabbas and Silas, two leaders among the brothers,
and sent them with this letter: The apostles and the elders, your brothers, To the brothers among the Gentiles in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia: Greetings.
It has come to our attention that some went out from us without our authorization and unsettled you, troubling your minds by what they said.
So we all agreed to choose men to send to you along with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,
men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Therefore we are sending Judas and Silas to tell you in person the same things we are writing.
It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us not to burden you with anything beyond these essential requirements:
You must abstain from food sacrificed to idols, from blood, from the meat of strangled animals, and from sexual immorality. You will do well to avoid these things. Farewell.

units.label: Joy at Antioch
units.note: the churches are strengthened and rejoice

verses.text: So the men were sent off and went down to Antioch, where they assembled the congregation and delivered the letter.
When the people read it, they rejoiced at its encouraging message.
Judas and Silas, who themselves were prophets, said much to encourage and strengthen the brothers.
After spending some time there, they were sent off by the brothers in peace to return to those who had sent them.
But Paul and Barnabas remained at Antioch, along with many others, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord.

peritemno.gloss: To circumcise. The demand at issue is that Gentiles be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to be saved. The council rejects circumcision as a requirement for salvation, since a right standing comes by grace through faith, not by the covenant marker of the flesh.

pistis.gloss: Faith, trust. Peter says God cleansed the Gentiles' hearts by faith, making no distinction between Jew and Gentile. Faith, not the law, is the means by which God purifies and accepts; the whole council turns on this word.

zygos.gloss: A yoke, a heavy burden laid across the shoulders. Peter calls the law as a means of salvation a yoke that neither the fathers nor the present generation could bear. To lay it on the Gentiles would be to test God and deny the gospel of grace.

charis.gloss: Grace, unearned favour. We are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are. This is the decisive confession of the council: salvation is a gift received by faith, the same for Jew and Gentile, and not a wage earned by keeping the law.

basic.context: The success of the Gentile mission raises a burning question. Men from Judea come to Antioch teaching that unless Gentiles are circumcised and keep the law of Moses, they cannot be saved. Paul and Barnabas dispute this fiercely, and the matter is taken to the apostles and elders in Jerusalem. After much debate, Peter recalls how God gave the Spirit to Gentiles by faith without the law, Paul and Barnabas tell of God's work among the nations, and James shows from the prophets that God always meant to gather Gentiles. The council rules that Gentiles are not bound by the law, asking only that they abstain from a few practices that would wound fellowship with Jewish believers. A letter is sent, and the church at Antioch rejoices.
basic.hermeneutics: This is the theological turning point of Acts. Read Peter's speech as the doctrinal core: God made no distinction, cleansing hearts by faith, and we are saved through grace, not the yoke of the law. James then anchors this in Scripture, Amos 9, and offers a pastoral solution. Distinguish the two things the council settles: the truth of salvation by grace, which is permanent, and the four abstentions, which serve peace and fellowship in a mixed church.
basic.originalLanguages: The debate turns on a few decisive words. The demand is that Gentiles be circumcised, peritemno, and keep the law. Peter answers that God cleansed their hearts by pistis, faith, refusing to lay on them a zygos, a yoke, that no one could bear. The confession that settles it is charis: we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are.
basic.typology: James reads the rebuilding of David's fallen tent, from Amos 9, as fulfilled in Christ, the son of David, whose risen reign gathers the remnant of Israel and the nations into one people. The Gentiles' inclusion is not an afterthought but the ancient purpose of God, foretold and now fulfilled.
basic.christ: The whole council rests on Christ. It is through the grace of the Lord Jesus that we are saved, Jew and Gentile alike. The rebuilt tent of David is the kingdom of the risen Son of David, and the door to that kingdom is opened by His grace, not by the law. To require the law for salvation would be to say Christ's grace is not enough.
basic.god: God is the one who made the choice to save Gentiles, who knows the heart, who gave the Spirit, who cleansed hearts by faith, and who long ago promised to gather the nations. The decision is not merely the church's; it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us. Salvation is God's gift of grace, offered on the same terms to all.
basic.crossReferences: Amos 9:11-12 is the prophecy James cites for the gathering of the Gentiles. Galatians 2 gives Paul's own account of this controversy and the gospel of justification by faith. Acts 10 records the Gentile Pentecost Peter recalls. Ephesians 2 shows Jew and Gentile made one in Christ, the wall broken down.
basic.oneStory: The council secures the gospel that drives the whole book: the ascended Christ saves the nations by grace through faith, apart from the law, and gathers Jew and Gentile into one people. Had the church bound the law on the Gentiles, the mission to the ends of the earth would have been strangled at the root. Instead the door of faith stands open, and the word keeps advancing.

context.literary:
Acts 15 sits at the exact middle of the book, and Luke builds it as a hinge. Everything before it asks how the gospel got from Jerusalem to Gentiles; everything after it follows Paul into the Greek world with the question settled. The chapter is a miniature trial. A charge is laid in verses 1 and 5, evidence is heard in verses 7 to 12, Scripture is brought as the decisive witness in verses 13 to 18, a verdict is given in verses 19 to 21, and the verdict is carried out by letter and messengers in verses 22 to 35.

The speeches are arranged in a deliberate order. Peter speaks from experience, verses 7 to 11, and recalls Cornelius, Acts 10. Barnabas and Paul then speak, but Luke gives them only one verse, 15:12, and fills it with signs and wonders rather than argument. James speaks last and speaks from the Bible, verses 13 to 21. Experience, then testimony, then text: Luke shows the church reasoning in the way a healthy church should.

Two small details reward attention. The assembly fell silent, verse 12, after a noisy start, since verse 7 speaks of much discussion. And the letter in verses 23 to 29 is drafted in the first person plural, with a formula of greeting that matches the opening of the letter of James, James 1:1. Luke is quoting a document, and the style reads like a genuine ancient circular letter, with its sender, recipients, explanation, instruction and farewell.

The unit ends where it began, in Antioch, verses 30 to 35. The chapter is a loop: a dispute leaves Antioch, goes up to Jerusalem, and returns as joy.
context.historical:
Most scholars place this meeting around AD 48 or 49, a decade or so after Pentecost, and after the first missionary journey of Acts 13 and 14. Jewish believers still made up the bulk of the church, and they lived inside a world where Gentiles who wished to join Israel's God were expected to be circumcised, Genesis 17:9-14. The men from Judea in verse 1 were not villains in their own eyes. Genesis 17 calls circumcision an everlasting covenant and extends it even to foreigners who join the household. Their argument had the plain sense of Scripture on its side, which is exactly why the council needed to wrestle so seriously.

The Pharisees in verse 5 had taken the Messiah on board without taking off their Pharisaic framework. Their concern for the law was zeal, and Paul had once shared it, Philippians 3:5-6.

In the Greek and Roman world, Gentile sympathisers already attended synagogues as God-fearers, as Acts 10:2 and 17:4 show. Jewish communities were scattered through every major city, and Moses was read aloud every Sabbath, which is the force of James's remark in verse 21. A Gentile convert to Christ would meet these synagogues, and these neighbours, in every town.

The four requirements in verse 20 also have a background. Leviticus 17 and 18 lay duties on both the Israelite and the foreigner living among them: no sacrifices to the goat idols, Leviticus 17:7, no eating of blood, 17:10-14, and no sexual immorality of the kind listed in 18:6-23. The four prohibitions track these chapters. Gentiles, whom the Law had always expected to share the land with Israel without being circumcised, are now asked to honour the same basic standards of the shared household.
context.canonical:
The council gathers several Old Testament streams and brings them to a point. Genesis 12:3 promised that all peoples on earth would be blessed in Abraham, and Genesis 15:6 said Abraham was counted righteous when he believed, before circumcision was given in Genesis 17. Paul builds on that order in Romans 4:9-12, and Galatians 2 to 3 gives the argument that Acts 15 supports from the church's side.

Peter's phrase about a yoke the fathers could not carry echoes the long Old Testament record of Israel's failures, and the promises that God would one day deal with the heart, Deuteronomy 30:6, Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 36:26-27. The cleansing of Gentile hearts by faith in verse 9 reads as the early arrival of that promise.

James's quotation from Amos 9:11-12 is the best known canonical link. Amos spoke of the fallen booth of David, and James takes it as God's own prophecy of the Messiah's rule reaching the nations. His next clause, 'who does these things that have been known for ages,' ties Gentile inclusion to a plan older than the church.

Later, the New Testament carries the decision forward in several directions. Acts 16:4 shows the decrees handed to the churches, and Acts 21:25 shows James restating them to Paul. Paul himself writes the matter out in Galatians 2 to 5, Romans 3:28-30 and Ephesians 2:11-22. On idol food he gives his own, more detailed counsel in 1 Corinthians 8 and 10, and the risen Christ rebukes Pergamum and Thyatira for idol food and immorality in Revelation 2:14 and 2:20.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wrote for readers who knew the church had Jews and Gentiles in it and who needed to know why that mix was neither an accident nor a compromise. He lets the reader see how the apostles decided: by hearing what God had visibly done, by testing it against the prophets, and by choosing a course that guarded both truth and love. The council is not presented as a legal ruling imposed from above, but as a Spirit led consensus reached after open argument.

He also wanted Gentile believers, who would read or hear Acts, to know that their place was never conditional. Nothing in the letter takes back a word of verse 11. And he wanted Jewish believers to know that their own heritage had not been disowned. Moses is still read in every Sabbath synagogue, verse 21, and nothing in the decision calls Jews to abandon their customs.

For readers in later generations, who face all kinds of pressure to add something to Christ as a condition of belonging, Luke intended the chapter to serve as a settled reference point: the Church does not demand more than grace, and it does not despise the conscience of the weaker brother.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records an event and a decision; it gives no template for how to hold a church council. The speakers, the order and the wording are historical. What carries forward is the principle that a church can settle hard questions together by listening to testimony and to Scripture, and that it may do so with the confidence of verse 28. The phrase there is not a blank cheque for any committee, since it rests on the clear work of God in Acts 10 and on the clear word of the prophets.

The four abstentions are descriptive of what that mixed church needed at that time. Many Christians treat them as permanent law, others as a temporary courtesy. Paul's later handling of idol food, 1 Corinthians 8 and 10, and Romans 14, suggests the letter was a wise accommodation to circumstances rather than a new Torah. What stays fixed is that nobody is to be asked to earn salvation by observing ritual, and that believers with stronger consciences should yield to weaker ones in love. The salvation clause is prescriptive for all time; the specific list is pastoral wisdom to be applied with discernment.

debates.question: Is the Jerusalem visit of Galatians 2 the same as the council of Acts 15?

views.label: Galatians 2 is the council of Acts 15
views.case: Both passages tell of Paul and Barnabas going up to Jerusalem to settle whether Gentiles must be circumcised, Galatians 2:1-5 and Acts 15:1-2, and both end with the apostles extending the right hand to the Gentile mission. Those who hold this view note that Paul's private meeting with the leaders in Galatians can be a separate session within the larger trip. The famous silence about the decree in Galatians is explained by its being a later pastoral arrangement.

views.label: Galatians 2 is the famine visit of Acts 11:30
views.case: Others point out that Paul in Galatians lists every contact with Jerusalem to prove he got his gospel independently, so a visit that omitted the decree would be hard to account for if it had already been issued. On this reading Galatians was written before the council, which explains why Paul never appeals to the decree to settle the circumcision question. Titus, a Greek, was not compelled to be circumcised, Galatians 2:3.

debates.bearing: Both views agree on the point that matters for Acts 15: the apostles themselves refused to add circumcision as a condition of fellowship, and Paul's gospel was recognised by the pillars of the church. The question affects how we date Galatians more than how we read the council.

debates.question: What were the four abstentions of verse 20 meant to be?

views.label: A ritual and cultural courtesy
views.case: The items track Leviticus 17 and 18, the rules for the foreigner who lived among Israel. The Gentile believers are asked to avoid the things that would make table fellowship with Jewish believers impossible, and James gives his reason in verse 21, that Moses is read in every city. The decision is about peace in a mixed church.

views.label: A moral and ethical list
views.case: Some manuscripts of Acts leave out the 'strangled' and add a form of the golden rule, which pushes the meaning toward ethics: avoid idolatry, murder or bloodshed, and sexual sin. Those who prefer this reading say all four are matters the Old Testament treats as serious in themselves.

views.label: A permanent minimum standard
views.case: Others hold the list binds believers in every age, pointing to Revelation 2:14 and 2:20. On this view the early church saw the list as a guard against idolatry and sexual sin in particular.

debates.bearing: Whichever view is taken, the letter itself says these are 'essential requirements' for fellowship, not conditions of salvation. Paul's later teaching in 1 Corinthians 10 shows that the underlying issue is idolatry and love for the conscience of the weak, which is why the principle outlasts the list.

study.originalLanguages:
Luke chooses his words with care in this chapter, and several carry the argument beyond the terms the basic study names.

In verse 7 the 'much discussion' is zetesis, a word for searching inquiry or dispute, from the same family as the 'sharp debate' of verse 2, where Luke uses stasis and zetesis together. The first word usually means a faction or an uprising, and it is a strong choice for a quarrel at Antioch. The same noun appears for a riot in 19:40. The church treated the crisis as serious enough to warrant a full inquiry rather than an easy compromise.

Peter says in verse 8 that God 'knows the heart,' using a single compound title, kardiognostes, literally 'heart knower.' The word has already appeared in the apostles' prayer at 1:24 when they chose Matthias. Peter takes the title the church has always used for the Lord and sets it against Jewish assumptions about who is clean. God sees hearts, and He saw faith in Gentile hearts. In verse 9 he adds that God cleansed them, from katharizo, which carries the vocabulary of ritual cleanness; the same verb was used in the voice from heaven in 10:15. Cleansing, which the law tied to rituals, is here tied to faith.

In verse 10 the charge that the Pharisees 'test God' uses peirazo, the verb behind Israel's testing of the Lord in the wilderness, a failure that Deuteronomy 6:16 warns against. To demand more than God has given is to repeat the old sin.

Peter's conclusion in verse 11 reverses the expected order of a Jewish speaker. We might have expected him to say Gentiles are saved as we are. He says we are saved just as they are, which puts Jews on the common ground of grace.

In verse 14 James says God took from the Gentiles a people, laos, 'to be His own,' and laos is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for Israel. The same word returns in the Lord's promise at Corinth, 18:10. Gentiles are now called by the name Israel once held.

In verses 16 and 17 Amos speaks of the 'fallen tent,' skene, and the Lord who will 'rebuild' and 'restore' it. In the Hebrew of Amos 9:12 the nations are those Israel may possess, while the Greek version James follows speaks of the remnant of men who may seek the Lord. The two readings differ very little in Hebrew: the consonants for Edom and for humankind are the same, and the verbs for possess and for seek differ by one letter. James follows the Greek form, and the apostolic council receives it as the Spirit's meaning.

Finally the formula of verse 28, 'It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us,' uses edoxen, the verb of official decision. Luke later calls the result dogmata, decrees, in 16:4.

typology.type: The fallen tent of David, Amos 9:11
typology.fulfillment: Amos looked past the ruin of David's dynasty to a restored house. James reads that restoration as the risen Messiah's reign, which Peter already announced at Pentecost, Acts 2:30-36. The correspondence is that a Davidic king stands once more, and the escalation is that his kingdom is no longer a national tent but a house filled with the nations, who are called by the name of the Lord, verse 17. The type falls short because the old booth was a political monarchy; the fulfilment is a spiritual kingdom, Luke 1:32-33, that spreads by the word and not by the sword.

typology.type: Circumcision of the flesh and of the heart
typology.fulfillment: Circumcision marked Abraham's household as God's covenant people, Genesis 17:11. Moses already spoke of a deeper circumcision, 'the LORD your God will circumcise your heart,' Deuteronomy 30:6. Paul says the true circumcision is of the heart by the Spirit, Romans 2:28-29, and in Christ believers were circumcised in a circumcision not made with hands, Colossians 2:11. Peter's cleansing of Gentile hearts by faith is the same truth in action. The sign pointed forward to something deeper. It falls short because a mark on the body could not change a heart, which is why requiring it for belonging missed what it signified.

The Torah was a gift, yet Peter calls it a yoke that neither the fathers nor the apostles could bear, verse 10. Jesus offers His own yoke: 'my yoke is easy and my burden is light,' Matthew 11:28-30. The escalation is that rest comes by coming to Him rather than by carrying the load. Paul urges the Galatians not to submit again to a yoke of slavery, Galatians 5:1. The type falls short only as a way to salvation; as a revelation of God's holiness the law still teaches, Romans 7:12.

typology.type: The foreigner among the people, Leviticus 17 and 18
typology.fulfillment: Leviticus gave the resident foreigner standing within Israel's camp with a short list of shared duties. The Gentile believers occupy a similar place, and the four requirements echo that list. In Christ the correspondence deepens: the foreigner is no longer a guest at the edge but a member of the household, Ephesians 2:19. The dividing wall is gone, Ephesians 2:14. The pattern falls short because the old foreigner stayed a foreigner, whereas the Gentile in Christ becomes a fellow citizen.

study.christ:
The council does not mention the name of Jesus often, but it is entirely about Him. The risen Lord has poured out His Spirit on Gentiles, and the question is whether anything more is needed to belong to Him.

Christ is first the sufficiency of grace. Peter's confession, 'we believe it is through the grace of the Lord Jesus that we are saved,' puts the whole weight on Him. Paul says the same in Galatians 2:16, where a person is justified through faith in Jesus Christ, not by works of the law. To insist on circumcision as a condition is, in Paul's blunt phrase, to be cut off from Christ, Galatians 5:2-4. The council protects the sufficiency of Christ.

Christ is next the rebuilt house of David. When James cites Amos, he is in effect saying that the Messiah promised to David has come, and his reign has begun. Peter said as much at Pentecost, Acts 2:30-36, and Paul preached the same at Antioch in Pisidia, Acts 13:34, citing the sure blessings promised to David. The Davidic king gathers the nations because He is Lord of all, Acts 10:36.

Christ is the one in whom the dividing wall falls. Ephesians 2:14-16 says He Himself is our peace, who has made the two groups one and has broken down the barrier. The Jerusalem Council is the church's first public application of that work. Jews and Gentiles are reconciled in one body through the cross. It is the same logic as Galatians 3:28, where there is neither Jew nor Greek, for all are one in Christ Jesus.

Finally Christ is the end of the law as a way of righteousness, Romans 10:4. That does not mean the law was worthless, only that its goal has arrived. This is the pattern: promise, then fulfilment, then freedom.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The passage does not say that the law is bad or that Jewish believers must stop keeping their customs. In Acts 16:3 Paul himself circumcises Timothy for the sake of the Jews in that region, and in 21:23-26 he joins a vow in the temple. The point is never whether a person may keep Jewish customs but whether such customs can be required as a ground of acceptance.
study.god:
The council tells us first that God is the one who acts, and the church follows. Peter's argument is not that the apostles decided Gentiles ought to be accepted but that God had already accepted them, verses 7 to 9. The sequence is gospel, faith, Spirit, cleansing, and only then the church's recognition. The doctrine behind this is that salvation begins with God's initiative and is received by faith as a gift.

God is the one who knows hearts, verse 8. This is not a vague omniscience but a particular kind of knowledge that bears on the church. He sees the faith in a Gentile heart that no human official can verify, and He bears witness to it by the gift of the Spirit. That gift is the visible proof, as it was at Cornelius' house, Acts 10:44-48, and again at Pentecost.

He is impartial. Peter says God made no distinction between us and them, verse 9. Deuteronomy 10:17 had already said that the Lord does not show partiality, and Romans 2:11 states that God has no favourites. Yet in the same breath Scripture says God chose Israel. The chapter holds both together: God is free to choose a people and He chooses them to bless all peoples, Genesis 12:3. Election serves universality.

He is faithful to what He said long ago. James cites the prophets and closes with the remark that these things have been known for ages, verse 18. The new thing is not a change of plan. God did not scramble to repair a failed Israel; He was always gathering the nations.

He is a God who works through the community. The words 'it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us' do not make the Spirit one voice among others, but show that the Spirit worked through discussion, testimony and Scripture, and the people recognised His mind.

He is also a God of peace and pastoral wisdom. The decree asks for sensitivity, not fear. Worship is shaped by this: the Church gathers as one family, saved by one grace, and learns to give up rights for the sake of brothers and sisters.

crossReferences.note: The covenant of circumcision with Abraham, called everlasting and extended to foreigners in the household. This is the strongest text the Pharisaic believers could cite, which is why the council had to answer it. Paul replies in Romans 4:9-12 that Abraham was counted righteous before the sign was given.

The prophecy James quotes. Amos looks beyond the collapse of David's house to its rebuilding, and to the nations who are called by the Lord's name. James follows the Greek form of verse 12, where the remnant of men seek the Lord, and treats it as an exact description of what God was doing among the Gentiles.

The Gentile Pentecost at Cornelius' house, to which Peter appeals in verses 7 to 9. The Holy Spirit fell on those who heard before any rite was performed. Peter argued then, as he does at the council, that those who had received the Spirit as the apostles had could not be denied the water of baptism.

Paul's own account of a meeting with the Jerusalem leaders about circumcision. Titus, a Greek, was not compelled to be circumcised, and the pillars recognised the grace given to Paul. Whether this is the same occasion as Acts 15 is debated, but the principle is identical.

The prohibition on eating blood, applied to the Israelite and to the foreigner who lives among them. It helps explain why 'blood' appears on the apostolic list in verse 20, and why Leviticus 17 and 18 are widely thought to stand behind the four requirements.

Moses promises that the Lord will circumcise the heart of His people so that they love Him with all their heart. It shows that the heart was always what mattered, and Peter's phrase about hearts cleansed by faith, verse 9, reads as the arrival of that promise for Jew and Gentile alike.

Jesus invites the weary to take His yoke, which is easy, and His burden, which is light. Peter's description of the law as a yoke too heavy to bear, verse 10, makes this invitation more striking. The rest Jesus gives comes by coming to Him.

Paul tells the Gentile readers that they were once far off but are now brought near through the blood of Christ, with the dividing wall of hostility torn down. It is the theological summary of what the council protected, one new humanity in place of two.

Paul says a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law, and asks whether God is the God of Jews only. He is God of Gentiles too, since there is one God. This is Peter's argument at the council, drawn out in letter form.

Years later James tells Paul that the decision about Gentile believers stands. The apostles had not forgotten it, and the leaders in Jerusalem still treat it as the settled arrangement, even as they ask Paul to show that he walks in obedience to the law as a Jew.

study.oneStory:
The council answers a question that the whole Old Testament leaves open: how will the promise to Abraham, that all families of the earth will be blessed, actually reach those outside the covenant community? From Genesis 12 onward the nations hover at the edge of the story. Babel scattered them, Genesis 11. Isaiah saw them streaming to Zion, Isaiah 2:2-3. Jonah was sent to Nineveh, and a few foreigners like Rahab and Ruth were drawn in. Acts 15 is where the church decides, under the Spirit, that the door is open without a threshold of ritual.

The council also settles a question left by Jesus' own commission. He told the disciples they would be His witnesses to the ends of the earth, Acts 1:8. Yet the church had to learn what that meant for how Gentiles were to be received. Acts 10 gave the first sign, and this chapter gives the doctrinal conclusion. After it, the mission is free to run: Paul sets out for Macedonia and Greece in the next chapters.

Looking back to Genesis, Abraham's faith is vindicated. He was counted righteous by trusting God before he was circumcised, so he is father of all who believe, Romans 4:11. Looking back to Sinai, the law is not discarded but understood as a tutor until Christ came, Galatians 3:24. And looking back to Eden, the long scattering of the peoples is being reversed in one body.

The story ends in Revelation 7:9, where a great multitude from every nation, tribe, people and language stands before the throne. No one in that crowd has earned a place by a mark on the body. Revelation 21:24 pictures the nations bringing their glory into the city. The Jerusalem Council is an early step on the road to that day, and its decision keeps the road open.

quiz.q: What was the question the council at Jerusalem had to settle?

options.text: Whether Gentiles must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to be saved.
options.note: Verses 1 and 5 state the exact question the council addressed.

options.text: Whether Gentiles could be admitted to the church at all.
options.note: Close, but Gentiles were already believers; the issue was whether the law and circumcision were required for salvation.

options.text: Which leader should have authority over the churches.
options.note: The council was about the terms of salvation, not a power struggle over leadership.

options.text: Whether Paul was a genuine apostle.
options.note: Paul's apostleship was not the question; the terms of Gentile salvation were.

quiz.q: What did Peter argue at the council?

options.text: That God saves Jew and Gentile alike by grace through faith, without the yoke of the law.
options.note: Verses 9 to 11 give Peter's core argument: cleansed by faith, saved by grace.

options.text: That God had given the Spirit to Gentiles just as to the Jews.
options.note: True and part of his case, but the point he drives to is salvation by grace, not law.

options.text: That Gentiles should keep a reduced version of the law.
options.note: Peter argued against laying the law's yoke on them at all, not for a lighter version.

options.text: That circumcision was still necessary for full acceptance.
options.note: Peter argued the opposite, that the law is a yoke no one could bear and salvation is by grace.

quiz.q: How did James support the decision from Scripture?

options.text: He cited the prophets that God would rebuild David's tent to gather the Gentiles who bear His name.
options.note: Verses 16 to 17 quote Amos 9 to show the Gentile ingathering was God's ancient plan.

options.text: He agreed that God was doing a new thing among the Gentiles.
options.note: He affirmed God's work, but his key move was grounding it in the prophets, not calling it merely new.

options.text: He appealed only to the miracles Paul and Barnabas reported.
options.note: The signs were mentioned, but James rested the case on the written word of the prophets.

options.text: He argued the Gentiles must first become Jews.
options.note: James concluded the opposite, that Gentiles turning to God should not be troubled with the law.

quiz.q: Why did the council ask Gentiles to abstain from a few things?

options.text: For the sake of fellowship and peace with Jewish believers, not as a means of salvation.
options.note: The abstentions serve the unity of a mixed church; salvation had already been settled as by grace.

options.text: Because these particular practices were especially offensive to Jewish consciences.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but the deeper aim was preserving fellowship, and salvation was never in view as earned.

options.text: To require Gentiles to keep the most important parts of the law for acceptance.
options.note: The requests were not conditions of acceptance; the council had just freed them from the law's yoke.

options.text: To make the Gentiles prove their sincerity before being saved.
options.note: Salvation was by grace through faith; the abstentions were about love and fellowship, not proving worth.

quiz.q: What does the council teach about salvation?

options.text: That Jew and Gentile alike are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, received by faith.
options.note: Verse 11 is the confession at the heart of the council: saved through grace, just as they are.

options.text: That God accepts Gentiles because He gave them the Spirit.
options.note: The Spirit's gift is evidence, but the ground stated is the grace of the Lord Jesus received by faith.

options.text: That grace gets a person started but the law must complete them.
options.note: The council rejected adding the law; salvation is by grace through faith from start to finish.

options.text: That salvation is earned by keeping the law of Moses.
options.note: This is precisely what the council denied, calling the law a yoke no one could bear.

quiz.q: How was the decision described when the letter was written?

options.text: It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us.
options.note: Verse 28 shows the council understood its verdict as the mind of the Spirit, not mere human opinion.

options.text: The apostles and elders agreed together after much discussion.
options.note: True, they did agree after debate, but the letter grounds it above all in the Holy Spirit's leading.

options.text: The majority voted and the minority submitted.
options.note: The text stresses Spirit-led consensus and shared agreement, not a bare majority vote.

options.text: Paul decided the matter on his own authority.
options.note: The decision was the whole council's, attributed to the Holy Spirit, not to Paul alone.

questions: The false teaching added circumcision and law-keeping to grace. Where are you tempted to add conditions to the gospel, as if grace alone were not enough?
Peter called the law a yoke no one could bear. What burdens are you carrying to try to earn a standing with God that Christ offers you by grace?
The council grounded its decision in Scripture, testimony, and the Spirit's leading. How does your church discern hard questions, and what could you learn from this pattern?
The freed Gentiles were asked to limit their liberty for the sake of fellowship. Where might love call you to give up a freedom so as not to wound another believer?
The letter brought great joy and encouragement to the church. How does the truth that you are saved by grace, not by your performance, bring you fresh joy today?

translationNotes.note: James quotes Amos 9:11-12, following the wording of the Greek Old Testament, to show that the gathering of the Gentiles was foretold by the prophets.

The four abstentions, from idol food, sexual immorality, strangled meat, and blood, echo the laws for foreigners in Leviticus 17 and 18 and safeguard table fellowship between Jewish and Gentile believers.

The BSB omits verse 34, going from verse 33 to verse 35, because the earliest and best manuscripts do not contain it. A later addition, reflected in the Textus Receptus and noted in the BSB footnote, reads that Silas decided to remain there; it is not part of the original text, so no verse 34 appears in this study.
